biography: Hund was a German theoretical physicist who taught in Leipzig, Jena, Frankfurt and Göttingen. He connected atomic and molecular spectra with quantum electronic states and shaped quantum physics through research, textbooks and teaching. He also studied the history of physics later in his career.
contributions: Formulated Hund's rules for the ordering of atomic electronic energy levels
Developed quantum descriptions of molecular orbitals and spectra with Mulliken and others
Made early investigations of quantum tunnelling in molecules

biography: Mulliken was an American chemical physicist based for much of his career at the University of Chicago. He applied quantum mechanics to molecular electrons, developed the molecular-orbital method and built an influential research school. His work on bonding and molecular electronic structure earned the 1966 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
contributions: Developed molecular-orbital methods for understanding chemical bonding through quantum electronic states
Investigated molecular electronic structure and spectra and developed associated nomenclature and classifications
Introduced interpretive tools for electronic structure, including Mulliken population analysis

biography: Slater was an American theoretical physicist trained at Harvard who led physics research at MIT and later worked at the University of Florida. He applied quantum mechanics to the electronic structure of atoms, molecules and solids, emphasizing practical calculations while developing influential research groups and textbooks.
contributions: Developed and popularized Slater-determinant representations of antisymmetric many-electron wavefunctions
Introduced Slater-type orbitals and screening rules for atomic electronic calculations
Developed practical local-exchange approximations and other methods for molecular and solid-state calculations

biography: Kronig was a Dresden-born theoretical physicist trained at Columbia who later worked in Groningen and Delft. He investigated atomic spectra, crystal electrons and linear response. He considered electron spin early but did not establish publication priority; his published work supplied lasting tools for quantum materials and optics.
contributions: Developed the Kramers–Kronig dispersion relations connecting dispersive and absorptive response
Developed the Kronig–Penney model of electrons in a periodic potential with William Penney
Investigated molecular spectra and electron spin during the development of early quantum theory

biography: Neddermeyer was an American experimental physicist trained at Caltech. His cosmic-ray research with Carl Anderson contributed to the discovery of the particle later identified as the muon. He subsequently worked on wartime nuclear experiments and continued research and university teaching, linking early particle discoveries with experimental nuclear physics.
contributions: Co-discovered the muon with Carl Anderson, extending knowledge of the particle content of cosmic rays
Contributed to experimental nuclear research, associated experimental methods and physics teaching

biography: Casimir was a Dutch theoretical physicist trained with Ehrenfest who worked in Leiden and later helped direct research at Philips. He investigated nuclear magnetic moments, superconductivity and electromagnetic fluctuations, connecting quantum theory with industrial research. He is particularly known for the predicted force associated with quantum vacuum fluctuations.
contributions: Predicted the Casimir force between ideal conducting boundaries arising from electromagnetic quantum fluctuations
Investigated retarded dispersion interactions with Polder, now called Casimir–Polder interactions
Studied superconducting thermodynamics and two-fluid descriptions with Gorter and others

biography: Weizsäcker was a German physicist and philosopher influenced by Heisenberg. His research addressed atomic nuclei, stellar energy and planetary formation. He later worked in Hamburg and within the Max Planck Society and pursued questions of scientific responsibility and peace, while his physical work influenced nuclear structure and astrophysics.
contributions: Developed a semi-empirical mass formula describing nuclear binding energies
Investigated stellar nuclear reactions and independently contributed to the theory of the carbon–nitrogen–oxygen cycle
Studied planetary-system formation and foundational questions in theoretical physics

biography: Hahn was an American experimental physicist who investigated nuclear magnetic resonance at Illinois and later taught for decades at Berkeley. His discovery of spin echoes and development of pulsed resonance methods made coherence and relaxation in spin systems accessible to precise experiments and provided important foundations for MRI.
contributions: Discovered spin echoes, revealing coherent information recoverable from some apparent dephasing processes
Developed pulsed nuclear magnetic resonance and free-induction-decay measurements
Established experimental methods important to magnetic-resonance spectroscopy and later MRI

biography: Kohn was an Austrian-born American theoretical physicist who escaped Nazi persecution as a teenager and studied in Canada and the United States. He later worked at UC San Diego and UC Santa Barbara, where he became the founding director of the Institute for Theoretical Physics. His development of density-functional theory earned the 1998 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
contributions: Established foundational theorems of ground-state density-functional theory with Pierre Hohenberg
Developed the self-consistent Kohn–Sham equations for electronic-structure calculations with Lu Jeu Sham
Made major contributions to semiconductor physics, metallic electronic structure and surface physics

biography: Mills was an American theoretical physicist educated at Columbia and Cambridge. He collaborated with Chen Ning Yang at Brookhaven and later taught for many years at Ohio State. His research concerned quantum field theory, alloys and many-body systems; the non-Abelian gauge theory published with Yang in 1954 became foundational to modern particle physics.
contributions: Established non-Abelian gauge-field theory with Chen Ning Yang, now called Yang–Mills theory
Investigated propagators and quantum methods for many-body systems
Studied alloy theory and advanced modern physical methods through books and teaching

biography: Hubbard was a British theoretical physicist trained at Imperial College who worked at Harwell and later IBM in the United States. He studied solids through simplified models retaining essential electronic interactions. His work shaped strongly correlated electron physics and many-body theory before his early death.
contributions: Introduced the Hubbard model combining electron hopping with local interactions
Developed theoretical methods and operator descriptions for electronic correlations
Investigated electron gases, magnetism and metal–insulator behaviour

biography: Mansfield was a British physicist educated in London who spent most of his academic career at Nottingham. Moving from solid-state NMR to spatial imaging, he developed methods for analysing gradient-encoded signals and acquiring images rapidly. He shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Paul Lauterbur.
contributions: Developed spatial encoding and mathematical analysis of NMR signals in magnetic-field gradients
Proposed and developed rapid MRI methods including echo-planar imaging
Helped turn the physical principles of NMR into spatial imaging for medicine

biography: Zweig was born in Moscow and moved to the United States as a young child. Trained with Feynman at Caltech, he proposed fundamental constituents of hadrons independently of Murray Gell-Mann. He later investigated neurobiology, cochlear mechanics and signal analysis at institutions including Los Alamos and MIT, connecting particle physics with biophysics.
contributions: Independently proposed hadronic constituents later known as quarks, calling them aces
Applied physical and mathematical methods to cochlear mechanics and auditory signals
Developed signal-processing methods associated with the continuous wavelet transform

biography: Sham is a Hong Kong-born American theoretical physicist educated in Britain who worked for many years at UC San Diego. With Kohn he developed a practical density-functional framework. His later research on many-body effects, optical properties and electron-spin control in semiconductors connects electronic-structure theory with quantum-information research.
contributions: Developed self-consistent auxiliary one-electron equations for ground-state density-functional calculations with Kohn
Investigated many-body effects, excitons and nonlinear optical processes in semiconductors
Studied electron spins and their optical control in semiconductor nanostructures
